world.eraEvidence: modern knowledge economy, digital distraction, 2016 onward
world.setting: open-plan offices, secluded study rooms, and stone lakeside retreats

worker.name: Knowledge Worker
worker.role: The everyman modern professional caught between constant shallow demands and the urgent need for deep focus
worker.look: A 32-year-old knowledge worker of slim build with neat dark hair, wearing a clean charcoal sweater and chinos.

jung.name: Carl Jung
jung.role: Psychologist exemplar who withdrew to Bollingen Tower to practice bimodal deep work without electricity
jung.look: A sturdy 50-year-old Swiss intellectual with receding grey hair, round wire spectacles, and a tweed waistcoat.

room.look: A rustic stone retreat room inspired by Bollingen Tower with wooden furniture, oil lamps, and no electrical cords.

library.look: A silent academic library with towering bookshelves, reading lamps, and long mahogany study tables.

objects.why: Central concept of knowledge output versus shallow activity
Wildly important goals and intense cognitive targeting
Primary instrument of reflexive digital interruption and attention fragmentation
Analog index cards, journals, and physical scoreboards tracking deep work hours
Time-blocking, 90-minute ultradian focus sessions, and shutdown deadlines
High-value algorithmic problem solving and technical craft
The digital workstation as a double-edged sword for creation and distraction
Cognitive defense against attention residue and workplace interruptions
Hard intellectual books and sustained long-form concentration
Finite daily cognitive reserves and deep work rationing

spine.claim: Modern knowledge work mistakenly conflates frantic digital connectivity and busyness with genuine economic productivity.
Deep focus is a rare and exponentially rewarded economic asset, while attention residue degrades cognitive performance.
Willpower alone is insufficient; mastering depth requires structured scheduling philosophies and business-like execution.
Sustained focus demands embracing boredom, quitting addictive network tools, and draining shallow busywork.
Deep work is an existential reclamation: choosing disciplined concentration builds a richer, more meaningful life.
